justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the asset across all three horizons, with the 1-day estimate anchored closest to recent trading levels and each successive horizon nudging slightly higher. At the 1-day horizon, the estimate of 239.5 is essentially a mean-reversion assumption — prices tend to stay close to where they are over very short windows, so I weighted recent price action heavily and assumed no major catalyst would materially shift the level overnight. The 1-week estimate of 241.0 incorporates a small positive drift consistent with the broader trend, while the 1-month estimate of 244.0 reflects a continuation of that drift compounded over a longer window, tempered by the expectation that mean-reversion forces and macro headwinds could limit upside.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At 1 day, the 90% interval of 232–247 is relatively tight because intraday and overnight volatility is bounded in most normal market conditions. By 1 week, the interval expands to 225–257, capturing the possibility of a meaningful move driven by scheduled economic data, earnings releases, or shifts in Federal Reserve communication. At 1 month, the interval of 210–278 is quite wide because over that horizon, macroeconomic regime shifts, geopolitical developments, and changes in market sentiment can all compound in ways that are genuinely difficult to anticipate.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these relatively wide bands. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in economic data — such as a sharp rise in unemployment claims or a contraction in manufacturing activity — could trigger a risk-off selloff that breaks below 210. A sudden escalation in geopolitical tensions or a surprise central bank policy move could have similar effects. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season or a dovish pivot from the Federal Reserve could generate momentum that carries prices well above 278 over the monthly horizon.

It is also worth acknowledging model limitations. These estimates are derived from historical volatility patterns and trend assumptions, and they implicitly assume that the statistical relationships of the recent past continue to hold. If market structure changes — for instance, if a liquidity crisis emerges or if a major institutional player unwinds a large position — the realized outcome could fall well outside any interval constructed from normal-market assumptions. These tail risks are real but inherently difficult to quantify with precision.
